patches.old: \Title{HARK: Human-Gated Authority-Typed Review Knowledge for LLM-Assisted Proposal Review}
patches.new: \Title{HARK: Authority-Typed Review Knowledge for Evidence-Bearing Document Review}
patches.reason: 扩展任务定位，移除尚未兑现的Human-Gated题名保证。

patches.old: \abstract{Large language models (LLMs) increasingly pre-screen technical documents before an expert signs off, yet expert review knowledge enters such systems as keyword rules, prompt checklists or retrieval over past reviews, and each route loses a property that high-stakes review needs: findings must trace to a rule and a document location, decision authority must match how deterministically a requirement can be checked, knowledge must grow from use, and that growth must stay under human control. We call this the \emph{review-knowledge ingestion problem} and study it for preliminary review of technical solution proposals at a large utility. We present HARK (Human-Gated Authority-Typed Review Knowledge), which answers the four properties with four mechanisms rather than one. Knowledge becomes a versioned package of verifiability-typed rules: \emph{hard} rules are owned by deterministic verifiers that produce located evidence, including absence evidence an LLM may never assert; \emph{hybrid} rules let verifiers locate candidate spans while the LLM judges only inside them, enforced by a tool-side evidence gate; \emph{soft} rules only raise items for judgement. A deterministic policy derives the suggested verdict; only the expert writes the final one. Expert decisions become an audited learned layer that may tune parameters and phrasing but never promotes a rule's tier. Implemented as a plugin of an open-source agent harness (28 rules, no separate backend), the design is evaluated with a deterministic judge that decides only inside verifier-located spans; all numbers below are conditional on that judge, not on a particular large model. It reaches F1 0.798 against 0.222 for a keyword baseline on 100 synthetic proposals with 253 planted defects, with no finding raised on a clean proposal and 85\% verdict agreement ($\kappa=0.76$); 80\% of the remaining misses reach the expert as open items, at the cost of under-calling 15 of the 70 defective proposals, four of them to a pass. Only 10 of 28 rules proved deterministically verifiable, and the four blocking rules least of all.}
patches.new: \abstract{Rule-governed document review requires explicit criteria, source-addressable evidence, and a distinction between provisional findings and accountable human disposition. We present HARK (Authority-Typed Review Knowledge), a plugin architecture that represents review criteria as rules with hard, hybrid, or soft operational authority. Deterministic verifiers produce checks and candidate spans; a positional evidence gate checks submitted quotations; a policy derives suggested verdicts; and decision records support feedback storage. Technical solution proposals are the sole empirical instantiation. On a fixed developmental regression corpus of 100 synthetic proposals with 253 planted defects, the combined configuration achieves micro-F1 0.798 versus 0.222 for a keyword baseline and 85\% policy-verdict agreement. Of 70 policy-non-Pass proposals, 15 are under-called and 10 receive Pass, including four of 23 expected Fail proposals. Sixty-eight of 85 misses enter pending review, without evidence of human resolution. Five development-team runs on three internal proposals demonstrate workflow and persistence, not independent review quality or learning gains. The evaluated snapshot does not enforce authenticated human approval, a complete effective-authority ceiling, or content-addressed configuration recovery. These remain target contracts rather than implemented guarantees. The contribution is an executable review architecture with bounded comparative results and explicit implementation boundaries.}

patches.old: Before a change to a large online service platform is built, its \emph{technical solution proposal}---a templated document describing background, architecture, interfaces, data flows, implementation plan and risk---must be reviewed by a small group of senior experts. The review is checklist-driven, the documents are highly templated, the consequences are real (the expert signs the opinion), and the knowledge is both specialised and changing. These properties make the preliminary review a natural target for LLM assistance; they also make the usual way of building that assistance fragile.
patches.new: Rule-governed, evidence-bearing document review combines three conditions: explicit review criteria, a source-addressable document, and a distinction between provisional findings and accountable human disposition. Checklist-based inspection provides a foundation for this task~\cite{fagan1976,lait2000}. The computational problem is not only to generate comments, but to represent which criteria a system can check, what evidence it can supply, and which decisions remain with a reviewer. We study technical solution proposals for a large utility's online service platform: documents describing intended architecture, interfaces, data flows, implementation plans, and risks before implementation. Assurance cases, compliance dossiers, and architecture designs are potential applications of the same task formulation, not domains validated in this study.
patches.reason: 给出三条件任务定义及方案评审阶段，其他领域仅列潜在应用。

patches.old: Our starting point is a failed first attempt. A monolithic prototype built in 2025 encoded 24 expert rules as a few keywords each and delegated everything else to an LLM through long prompts. ``Load test'' appearing anywhere counted as the load test having been planned; negations (``no load test is planned for now''), placeholders (``/'', ``N/A'') and empty sections were invisible; the verdict was whatever the model wrote into a single field, so a blocking finding did not change the outcome; and nothing was persisted, so the hundredth review was no better informed than the first. A faithful reimplementation of that design, evaluated below on the same corpus as the design we propose, recovers 18.6\% of planted defects, produces 2.6 false findings for every true one, and agrees with the expected verdict no better than chance ($\kappa=-0.04$). None of this was a failure of the model. All of it was a failure of \emph{how the review knowledge had been put into the system}.
patches.new: The motivating prototype represented 24 expert rules through keyword lists and prompts, without a persistent feedback layer. This arrangement made it difficult to distinguish a requirement's mention from its satisfaction or to connect a proposed finding to an inspectable decision path. Its keyword component is represented by baseline B0 in the evaluation. On the fixed synthetic corpus, B0 recovers 18.6\% of planted defects, produces 124 false findings against 47 true findings, and achieves policy-verdict agreement of $\kappa=-0.043$. These results motivate a different representation and routing architecture; they do not identify model failure or isolate the causal contribution of typing.
patches.reason: 撤回原型历史与模型无错的绝对归因，准确限定B0比较。

patches.old: Take a single rule, ``a load test must be planned before go-live''. In a corpus of real proposals written for this platform, the sentence that satisfies it reads: ``Load testing is completed by the test team one week before go-live and a report is issued.'' Three other formulations appear just as often. The negated one: ``No stress testing is planned for the time being; it will be decided after observing traffic after go-live.'' The hollow one: ``Load testing plan: to be determined'', or ``Load testing: /''. And the satisfied-by-analogy one, in which the required content exists but the keyword family does not: ``Before go-live we run the capacity drill in the pre-production environment; at 500 TPS the average response time must stay below 200 ms.'' All four contain the keyword that a rule-as-substrings implementation keys on. Only one of them is a pass, and the difference between them is not a difference in wording but in what part of the document they occupy and what a reader does with them.
patches.new: Consider the criterion that a proposal specify load testing before go-live. ``No load test is planned'' and ``Load testing plan: to be determined'' mention the activity without supplying an adequate plan. Conversely, ``A pre-production capacity drill will measure response time at 500 TPS before go-live'' may provide relevant evidence without the phrase ``load test''. These illustrative formulations separate lexical presence, document location, and substantive satisfaction. A deterministic cue can support a limited check or identify a passage for review; it does not by itself establish that a testing plan is sufficient.
patches.reason: 修复所有示例均含关键词的矛盾，明确词法代理与业务充分性不同。

patches.old: Three ingestion routes dominate practice, and each loses a different property. \emph{Keywording} turns a rule into substrings and loses its meaning: presence is not satisfaction and absence is not violation. \emph{Prompting} turns a rule into instructions and loses auditability: the model has seen the rule, but its judgement cannot be traced to the rule or to a document location. \emph{Fragmenting}---retrieval over past reviews---loses accumulation: knowledge is reassembled at every query and never consolidated. All three treat knowledge as input shown to the model rather than as an asset owned by the system, and all three make the same implicit assumption, that a requirement can be handed to a single mechanism.
patches.new: We call the representation and routing task the \emph{review-knowledge ingestion problem}: how should review criteria, evidence expectations, and decision permissions enter an assisted review system? Keyword checks offer reproducible surface tests; prompts convey contextual instructions; retrieval supplies relevant prior material. None of these mechanisms alone specifies the complete contract linking a criterion, a document range, a proposed finding, and its disposition. HARK combines them through explicit rule records and review states rather than treating the model's output as the final decision.
patches.reason: 不再对关键词、提示、检索作无来源的全称负能力断言，转为具体契约问题。

patches.old: Two tensions underlie that assumption. The \emph{verifiability tension}: requirements span a spectrum from ``the implementation-plan section exists and is not a placeholder'', which a program can check exactly, to ``the risk analysis is adequate'', which is almost entirely judgement. The less verifiable a requirement, the more it needs a model; the more verifiable it is, the less a model should be trusted with it, because models make unexplained errors on deterministic questions and cannot locate them~\cite{liu2024lost,huang2024self}. A representation that assigns every rule to one mechanism must therefore be wrong for most of the rule set, and the error is not random: it concentrates on exactly the rules an organisation cares about most. The \emph{growth tension}: knowledge must grow from use---every dismissal is information---but where a human signs the outcome, growth cannot be unilateral, and growth in weights or filter thresholds is invisible to those accountable for it.
patches.new: Two design tensions guide the architecture. First, review criteria mix observable structure with contextual judgement: section presence can be checked mechanically, whereas risk adequacy requires interpretation. Verifiability is therefore relevant to routing~\cite{iso29148,genova2013}, but the ability to execute a lexical test must not be confused with complete decidability of its business requirement. Second, useful decision history may inform later reviews, yet recording a decision, authorising a knowledge change, and demonstrating improved review quality are different accomplishments. A system must expose these boundaries rather than infer human approval from a name or infer learning benefits from stored feedback.

patches.old: We present HARK, an open-source implementation of this representation as a plugin of an open agent harness, and evaluate it on a synthetic corpus of 100 proposals and on three internal proposals reviewed in five sessions end to end. We make four contributions:
patches.new: We present HARK (Authority-Typed Review Knowledge) as a plugin for an open-source agent harness and examine its design, evaluated implementation snapshot, and validation boundaries. The paper makes four contributions:
patches.reason: 统一名称及系统设计实现验证路线。

patches.old:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=*]
\item We formulate the \emph{review-knowledge ingestion problem} and derive four design requirements for a solution---\emph{auditability}, \emph{authority follows verifiability}, \emph{growth}, \emph{bounded growth}---together with the mechanism that enforces each requirement and the instrument that measures it (Table~\ref{tab:reqs}).
\item A \emph{verifiability-typed} rule model in which the type decides who may raise a finding: hard rules are owned by deterministic verifiers, hybrid rules admit the model only inside verifier-located spans, and soft rules only queue items for the expert. Absence is a verifier-owned evidence kind, candidates are never a pass, and a deterministic policy computes the suggested verdict from confirmed findings alone (Section~\ref{sec:rules}, Figure~\ref{fig:type}).
\item \emph{Review as feedback}: the expert's ordinary review decisions---accept, dismiss, rewrite, add---are the only source of change to a learned layer that the system may tune but never promote, with an effective knowledge version stamped on every review (Section~\ref{sec:feedback}).
\item A plugin-native implementation with no separate backend, database or front-end build, evaluated on a released synthetic corpus with planted defects against a faithful reimplementation of the keyword prototype, including per-tier, per-severity, per-defect-kind and threshold analyses, an evidence-gate audit and an end-to-end walkthrough (Section~\ref{sec:results}).
\end{enumerate}
patches.new:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\arabic*),leftmargin=*]
\item A task formulation for rule-governed, evidence-bearing document review and a rule representation that separates evidence production, provisional findings, suggested verdicts, and human disposition (Section~\ref{sec:problem}).
\item An operational authority model with hard, hybrid, and soft routes, verifier-produced absence records, quotation checks, and a deterministic verdict policy, together with the limits of those routes in the evaluated snapshot (Sections~\ref{sec:rules}--\ref{sec:policy}).
\item A plugin-native implementation with feedback records, overrides, exemplars, and review-state storage, distinguished from the target contracts for authenticated approval, complete effective-authority control, and content-addressed recovery (Sections~\ref{sec:feedback} and~\ref{sec:impl}).
\item A fixed synthetic end-to-end regression comparison, a traceability and pending-workload analysis, and development-team workflow evidence from three internal proposals in five runs (Section~\ref{sec:results}).
\end{enumerate}

patches.old: The design is assessed one question per property: \textbf{RQ1} can every finding be traced to a rule and a location in the document? \textbf{RQ2} does typed authority outperform untyped authority, and does the type predict where the remaining judgement sits? \textbf{RQ3} does the knowledge measurably grow, and \textbf{RQ4} is all growth human-attributable and reversible? Section~\ref{sec:results} answers RQ1 and RQ2 with measurements on the released corpus, reports what RQ3 and RQ4 would require, and states explicitly which of the four properties this study does not yet measure.
patches.new: Four research questions organise the evaluation. \textbf{RQ1:} How are review knowledge and operational authority represented, and where are the implementation boundaries? \textbf{RQ2:} What detection and verdict trade-offs do the end-to-end configurations exhibit on the fixed synthetic corpus? \textbf{RQ3:} What traceability and gate-acceptance evidence is available, and what unresolved workload is routed to human review? \textbf{RQ4:} What evidence supports decision persistence, human approval, and version recovery, and which gaps remain? RQ2 concerns a combined-configuration comparison, not the causal effect of typing; RQ4 concerns workflow and recovery evidence, not online improvement.
patches.reason: 统一四个RQ，避免章节间换题与typing或学习效果偷换。

patches.old: Figure~\ref{fig:arch} summarises the resulting architecture. A proposal enters as Markdown (Word and PDF are converted upstream); the parser produces a structured document with source offsets; verifiers own everything that can be decided deterministically and prepare candidate spans for everything that cannot; the model sees only those spans and may only propose findings; the evidence gate admits a finding only if its quotation can be located inside the span the verifier chose; the policy turns confirmed findings into a suggested verdict; and the only path back into knowledge is the expert's decisions, which are written to an audited learned layer.
patches.new: Figure~\ref{fig:arch} outlines the architecture. A Markdown document is parsed into source-addressable structures; verifier checks produce findings or candidate spans; a judge submits quotations; a gate checks their location; and a deterministic policy derives a suggested verdict from eligible findings. Decisions and feedback are stored separately. In the evaluated snapshot, the gate tests candidate overlap rather than strict containment, gate-confirmed findings can affect the recommendation before human adoption, and the final-verdict tool requires a reviewer string rather than authenticated approval. The stricter separation of authority and complete configuration recovery described as target contracts are not implemented guarantees.
patches.reason: 图前明确快照实际语义，避免架构图被读为已落实强保证。

patches.old: \caption{Architecture and the direction of authority. Solid arrows move a proposal through the review; dashed arrows are the only path by which knowledge changes. Hard checks are decided inside the verifier layer and never reach the model; the model may only propose a finding inside a span the verifier chose, and the gate rejects it if the quotation does not lie there. The learned layer may tune parameters, phrasing, severity and status of shipped rules and may draft new soft rules, but it cannot promote a rule's tier; a change to severity or status is refused unless it quotes the expert's own instruction and is listed in the opinion it affects, so no dashed path widens what the system may settle alone.}
patches.new: \caption{Review architecture and intended feedback flow. Solid arrows depict document processing; dashed arrows depict decision and knowledge-update paths. The diagram summarises the design, not a verified security boundary. The evaluated gate checks quotation location and candidate overlap; tool-entered reviewer names and instruction quotations do not authenticate human approval. Controls covering all authority-changing operations and immutable effective-configuration snapshots remain target contracts.}
